newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Blasts overnight, but Zaire's second city calm.
newsitem.headline: Blasts overnight, but Zaire's second city calm.

text.p: Explosions were reported overnight on approaches to Zaire's second city, but the new day dawned calm.

Mortar fire exploded on Monday night on the southern approaches and witnesses reported hearing blasts at around midnight northeast of Lubumbashi, which has been declared the next main target by rebels fighting to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Explosions first erupted around 8.45 p.m. and continued into the night, interspersed with the rattle of multi-barrelled rocket launchers. A military expert said it sounded like incoming 120mm mortar fire landing about seven km (four miles) south of the city.
There were few people on the streets on Tuesday morning after the overnight curfew ended at 6 a.m. and some soldiers milled about aimlessly.
Nightwatchmen who had been guarding buildings said there had been a few explosions in the direction of the airport, northeast of the city, around midnight.
Soldiers manning a roadblock said government troops fought off rebels near Kipushi, 30 km (20 miles) southwest of Lubumbashi.
"Everything is calm. We repulsed the enemy near Kipushi," one soldier said. There was no independent confirmation of this.
Rebels trying to end Mobutu's 32-year rule have met little resistance since launching their armed campaign from Zaire's eastern borderlands six months ago.
The heavy gunfire suggested staunchly loyal elements of Mobutu's collapsing army of ill-paid and demoralised troops had decided to put up a last stand in Lubumbashi.
International efforts to negotiate an end to the fighting showed no sign of a breakthrough after a third day of talks on Monday between warring parties in South Africa.
Lubumbashi is the capital of Zaire's lifeline copper and cobalt mining industry that has underpinned Mobutu's hold on the vast Central African country.
Earlier on Monday a Zairean government army commander said the rebels were about 15 km (10 miles) from the city.
In the capital Kinshasa Defence Ministry sources said Zaire's Special Presidential Service forces (DSP) had been sent to push back rebels from Kipushi, on the Zambian border.
The fall of Kipushi could not be directly confirmed, but business people in Lubumbashi said the news had come directly from residents of the town contacted by telephone.
In South Africa envoys from Kinshasa and those of rebel leader Laurent Kabila met through Monday with no tangible sign of any progress in the search for peace.

"What's been happening is the Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and other (South African) representatives spent all day conferring with the leadership of both parties, separately and jointly," a South African spokesman told Reuters.
The spokesman declined to say what progress had been made or when the participants might be ready to make a statement.

In Kinshasa supporters of Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi defied armoured vehicles and teargas to prevent a parliamentary debate of no-confidence in the controversial politician who took office only last week.

The protesters failed to enter the assembly building but dispersed leaving it surrounded by gendarmes, some of whom openly supported Tshisekedi. The building was under the control of hundreds of troops but with no parliamentarians inside.
Tshisekedi, Mobutu's chief political rival, was appointed last week but parliament has initiated moves to remove him because of his unilateral decision to dissolve the assembly.
Tshisekedi supporters planned more protests for Tuesday.
